title: How the F1 Budget Cap Changed Everything — and Whether It's Working
summary: Formula 1's cost cap was introduced to level the playing field between rich and poor teams. Five years on, we assess what has changed, what hasn't, and whether the sport is genuinely more competitive as a result.
content:
For most of Formula 1's history, the sport operated on a simple principle: spend more, go faster. The teams with the biggest budgets — Ferrari, McLaren, Red Bull, Mercedes — dominated because they could afford to. Smaller teams were competing for points, not victories. The gap between the front and the back of the grid was not just sporting — it was financial.

The introduction of the budget cap in 2021 was the most significant structural change to Formula 1 in decades. It set a limit on how much teams could spend on car development. And it was supposed to change everything.

What the Cap Was Meant to Do

The logic was straightforward: if you limit spending, you limit the advantage that wealthy teams can buy. A McLaren or an Alpine, spending at the cap, would be closer to a Red Bull or Mercedes, also spending at the cap. The gap would narrow. The racing would improve.

In theory, the cap made competitive sense. In practice, it has been more complicated.

The Loopholes and the Exceptions

The budget cap has never been a pure spending limit. Marketing costs, driver salaries, and the top three employees' wages at each team are excluded. This means that the total amount wealthy teams spend on their F1 operations remains vastly higher than the nominal cap figure.

Red Bull's 2021 cap breach — found to have overspent by a relatively small amount — caused enormous controversy and raised questions about policing. How do you audit the accounts of multinational corporations with complex structures? The FIA's ability to enforce the cap has been questioned by critics who believe the system relies too heavily on self-reporting.

The budget cap was the right idea. Whether it has been implemented with enough rigour to genuinely equalise competition is a harder question to answer honestly.

Has Competition Improved?

The honest answer is: somewhat. The gap between the top three teams and the midfield has narrowed compared to the pre-cap era. Teams like McLaren and Ferrari have been able to close the gap to Red Bull in a way that would have been extremely difficult — perhaps impossible — without spending restrictions.

But the front of the grid is still dominated by the same teams it has always been dominated by. Red Bull won a historic number of races in 2023. Mercedes remain competitive. Ferrari have the resources to hire the best engineers. The fundamental hierarchy has not been overturned.

The Verdict

The budget cap is an imperfect solution to a genuine problem. It has made Formula 1 more competitive at the margins without fundamentally reshaping the competitive order. For fans who want to see genuine unpredictability — different teams winning races, genuine title fights involving four or five constructors — there is still work to do.

But the direction of travel is right. And in a sport that changes slowly, that matters.
